title: I used AI across most of development on two shipped iOS games. What was hardest to take from prototype to release?
author: JrFlexible
selftext:
I'm the developer of Blood Exile and FENER: Fogbound Lighthouse, two free iOS games. AI tools were involved in most parts of making both games, not just one isolated task. I want to be upfront about that rather than present them as fully human-made.



Blood Exile is a short dark-fantasy action roguelite: you move through a horde, choose support gems that change your attack, then face a boss during a run of up to six minutes.



FENER is a lighthouse-defense roguelite: you aim the beam to slow and damage enemies while the cannon fires automatically, then build through 30 waves.



Getting an AI-assisted project to a released game is a different question from getting a prototype to run. I'm interested in what other developers found hardest when turning AI-assisted output into a coherent, playable release.



Blood Exile: [https://blood-exile.pages.dev/](https://blood-exile.pages.dev/)

FENER: [https://fener.pages.dev/en](https://fener.pages.dev/en)

comments.author: aigamedev-mod
comments.body: u/JrFlexible could you add more about how AI fit into your development process? Just mentioning that AI was used doesn't cut it. Under Rule 4, promotional posts need to contribute something by discussing how the game was actually made. Otherwise the sub gets buried in ads. If there's no update, this post may be removed.

replies.author: JrFlexible
replies.body: Thanks for pointing this out. You’re right; my original post only mentioned AI without explaining how it fit into development. I’ve updated the post with more detail about how I worked with Claude and Codex and what my role was. The hardest part has actually been publishing and marketing the games, especially getting them in front of players
